title: Checkpoint: The Internet
objective: After this level you can trace a message from your device across the internet and explain how it stays private.
summary: A message leaves by Wi-Fi radio, travels as encrypted packets, crosses oceans as light in fiber and is rebuilt at the far end. Light in fiber takes about 5 millionths of a second per kilometer.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: how long does your message take to cross an ocean?
cards.body: You tap Send. Your words leave by radio, cross the seabed as flashes of laser light in glass fiber and arrive on another continent. Put the whole chapter together and the answer is a small fraction of a second: about a twentieth for 10,000 km of fiber.

items.label: Leaving home
points: Wi-Fi radio carries it to your router (Level 64)
It travels as packets over any available route (Level 62)

items.label: On the way
points: TCP numbers the packets and resends lost ones

items.label: Arriving
points: The receiver puts the packets back in order
Only the right key unlocks the contents

cards.headline: Light, slowed down by glass
cards.body: In empty space, light crosses a kilometer in about 3.34 millionths of a second. Glass slows it: in optical fiber it takes about 4.9 millionths, usually rounded to 5. That's about two-thirds of its top speed. Level 3's electrical push also raced through wires at nearly the speed of light. In fiber, the signal is the light itself.

cards.fact: Every 1,000 km of fiber adds about 5 thousandths of a second.
cards.context: At 5 millionths of a second per kilometer, 1,000 km takes 5 thousandths of a second, and a 10,000 km trip takes about a twentieth of a second, one way. Physics sets that floor: the light can't go any faster through the glass.

mascot.line: Halfway around the planet in a twentieth of a second. And somehow the loading spinner still finds time to spin.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: How a message crosses the world: chopped into packets, sent by any route, and rebuilt at the other end.
What really carries the data: Wi-Fi radio for the last hop and laser light in undersea cables.
Why the internet and the web are different things, and how a search engine finds pages before you ask.
How encryption lets strangers keep secrets, and why long, unique passwords and a second factor protect you.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long does light take to travel through 1,000 km of optical fiber?
questions.explanation: At about 5 millionths of a second per kilometer, 1,000 km takes about 5 thousandths of a second.

questions.prompt: Why does light travel slower through an undersea fiber than through empty space?

options.label: Seawater pushes back against it
options.rationale: The light is inside the glass; the glass slows it.

options.label: It travels as electric current, not light
The glass of the fiber slows it down
It stops at every packet to check the address
options.rationale: Speed in fiber is set by the glass itself.

questions.explanation: Light in optical fiber takes about 4.9 millionths of a second per km instead of 3.34 in a vacuum: the glass slows it to about two-thirds.

questions.prompt: Tracing an internet message from your home: which stretch usually travels by radio rather than by cable?

options.label: From your device to your home router
Across the ocean floor
options.rationale: That's laser light in glass fiber (Level 63).

options.label: Between continents, by satellite
options.rationale: Over 99% of that data goes by undersea cable.

options.label: Inside the data center's cooling pipes
options.rationale: Cooling pipes carry heat away, not messages.

questions.explanation: Wi-Fi uses radio waves for the short hop between your device and the router; the long stretches run on cables.

questions.prompt: From Level 62: how do the packets of one internet message travel?

options.label: All together on one reserved line
In one piece, never split up
options.rationale: Packet switching splits the message up.

options.label: Only by satellite
options.rationale: Most long-haul data goes by cable (Level 63).

questions.explanation: Each packet carries its destination address and travels independently; the message is reassembled at the end.

questions.prompt: From Level 68: in public-key encryption, what can anyone holding your public key do?

options.label: Lock a message that only your private key can open
Read every password stored in your password manager
options.rationale: A public key only locks; it reveals nothing.

options.label: Break Caesar's cipher faster
options.rationale: Caesar's cipher falls to trying 25 shifts; keys don't matter.

questions.explanation: Public-key cryptography uses two keys: the public one locks, and only the matching private key unlocks.
